stemMd: Phosphoric acid, $\mathrm{H_3PO_4}$, has three hydrogen atoms that can be replaced by sodium. A solution containing 0.50 mol of $\mathrm{H_3PO_4}$ reacts completely with 1.0 mol of $\mathrm{NaOH}$, with no reagent left over. Which salt is formed?
explanationMd:
Sodium hydroxide replaces the hydrogens of the acid one at a time, so the mole ratio of base to acid tells you how many hydrogens have been replaced.

$$\mathrm{H_3PO_4 + NaOH \rightarrow NaH_2PO_4 + H_2O}\qquad (1:1)$$
$$\mathrm{H_3PO_4 + 2\,NaOH \rightarrow Na_2HPO_4 + 2\,H_2O}\qquad (1:2)$$
$$\mathrm{H_3PO_4 + 3\,NaOH \rightarrow Na_3PO_4 + 3\,H_2O}\qquad (1:3)$$

The amounts are 1.0 mol of base for 0.50 mol of acid, a ratio of $1.0 \div 0.50 = 2$. Two hydrogens are replaced and one remains, giving $\mathrm{Na_2HPO_4}$ (disodium hydrogen phosphate).

**Check the charges:** two $\mathrm{Na^+}$ give $+2$, and the anion $\mathrm{HPO_4^{2-}}$ gives $-2$, so the salt is neutral. Check the atoms too: 1 P, 4 O, 1 H remain in the salt, and the 2 H removed leave with the 2 OH as 2 $\mathrm{H_2O}$.

distractorRationale.c: This replaces only one hydrogen, which needs one mole of $\mathrm{NaOH}$ per mole of acid. Here the ratio is 1.0 mol : 0.50 mol, that is two moles of base per mole of acid.
distractorRationale.e: This replaces all three hydrogens, which would need three moles of $\mathrm{NaOH}$ per mole of acid, or 1.5 mol of base here. Only 1.0 mol is available.
distractorRationale.a: This is not a charge-balanced formula, so no such neutral salt exists. It puts in the right two sodiums but also strips off the remaining hydrogen, leaving the phosphate ion: $2\times(+1)$ from sodium and $-3$ from $\mathrm{PO_4^{3-}}$ give a net charge of $-1$. Two sodiums replace two hydrogens, so one hydrogen must stay, giving $\mathrm{Na_2HPO_4}$.
distractorRationale.b: This is not a charge-balanced formula either, so no such neutral salt exists. It keeps the right anion for two replaced hydrogens, $\mathrm{HPO_4^{2-}}$, but pairs it with only one $\mathrm{Na^+}$, leaving a net charge of $-1$. Counting sodium atoms instead of charges misleads here: the anion $\mathrm{HPO_4^{2-}}$ needs two $\mathrm{Na^+}$.

independentSolve.workingNotes: The mole ratio NaOH:H3PO4 is 2:1, so two H are replaced, giving Na2HPO4 (H3PO4 + 2NaOH -> Na2HPO4 + 2H2O). NaH2PO4 needs a 1:1 ratio and Na3PO4 needs 3:1. [A second, separate blind solve (blind-reviewer-wave6-tolcf-chem-run18) reached the same answer: A 1:2 acid-to-NaOH ratio replaces two hydrogens and gives Na2HPO4. NaH2PO4 would need a 1:1 ratio, and Na3PO4 a 1:3 ratio. Na2PO4 and NaHPO4 are not charge-balanced formulas.]
